extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and practitioners handling claim construction (Markman) disputes in federal courts and concurrent USPTO proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for construing patent claim terms (Markman practice) in federal court, including use of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, drafting Markman briefs, conducting Markman hearings, and managing concurrent USPTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a question of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a question of law reserved for the court and not a question of fact left to the fact finder (Markman v. Westview Instruments Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal, the Federal Circuit generally reviews district, ITC and USPTO claim determinations de novo; for district court constructions the Federal Circuit gives no deference to district court factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step process for infringement determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement requires a two-step process: the court must construe the patent claims, then the fact finder must evaluate the construed claims against the allegedly infringing device or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity determinations likewise depend on the construed patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with intrinsic evidence; extrinsic only as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper claim construction requires review of the patent's intrinsic evidence and, when appropriate, extrinsic evidence (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence is primary; extrinsic evidence may be used only if helpful and must not vary or contradict intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence components
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence includes: the claims, the specification and the prosecution history (See Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1314).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review disputed claim terms in light of the intrinsic evidence because a POSA reads claim terms in the context of the particular claim and the entire patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning to a POSA
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA), if possible (Vitronics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A POSA is a fictional, objective person having the average knowledge, skill and expertise in the claimed invention's technical or scientific field (Phillips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context within the claim and claim differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The context in which terms appear in the claim as a whole is important; different terms used to identify similar limitations should have different meanings (Bancorp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will attach different meanings to words/phrases used in separate claims (claim differentiation), but this presumption can be overcome by specification or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claim parts (preamble, transitional phrases, limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may consider the preamble, transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising' vs 'consisting of'), and the claim limitations when construing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble may limit the claim where it recites essential structure or is necessary to give 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim; 'comprising' is generally open-ended while 'consisting of' is limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification is highly relevant and can be dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is always highly relevant to claim construction and is usually dispositive where the proposed construction aligns with the patent's description (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specification where it describes preferred/sole embodiments, distinguishes prior art, or defines terms; but avoid improperly importing limitations from the specification into the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper claim construction should capture the scope of the actual invention and should not: limit the scope of the claims to the disclosed embodiment or allow claim language to become divorced from what the specification conveys is the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious where specification describes embodiments—distinguish legitimate guidance from improper limitation (Retractable Techs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee can act as lexicographer but must do so clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is free to provide any definition for a claim term, often in the specification, but must clearly indicate the desired definition to overcome the presumption that ordinary meaning applies (Vitronics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear indication can include explicit definitions or typographical cues (e.g., quotation marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history can show disclaimer but is less authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history—the written record of correspondence with the USPTO—can provide helpful information (e.g., showing that the patentee disclaimed a broad definition) but often lacks the clarity of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and unambiguous disclaimer in prosecution history supports limiting construction (Omega Eng'g); courts treat prosecution history as often less helpful than specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence types and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (anything not within the patent or prosecution history) can include dictionaries, treatises and expert testimony and may be used to inform relevant scientific principles, technical term meanings, and state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court has no obligation to consider extrinsic evidence and must not use it to vary or contradict intrinsic evidence (Phillips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries and treatises carry weight and should be contemporaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has given dictionaries and treatises more weight than other forms of extrinsic evidence (Vitronics). Because claims are interpreted using the definition known to a POSA at the time of invention, the dictionary or treatise should include a definition from that time (Symantec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select authoritative, contemporaneous sources when relying on dictionaries/treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony is primarily background; rarely determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony can provide background, explain how an invention works, ensure the court's understanding matches a POSA, and establish term meanings in the field (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on expert testimony to construe terms is proper only in rare instances where intrinsic evidence, taken as a whole, does not enable construction (Vitronics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is case-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of a claim term in one case may be completely different from that same term in another case, especially where fields of technology differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider the particular intrinsic/extrinsic record and POSA context for the case at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve claim validity when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should preserve the claims' validity, except where an invalidating construction is consistent with the claim language and specification (based on the presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. §282).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction should not be unduly narrow or broad if that conflicts with patent text and specification (Marine Polymer; Rhine).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO uses the broadest reasonable interpretation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction rule in USPTO proceedings applies the broadest reasonable interpretation to the claims, differing from district court approaches (In re Yamamoto).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize divergent standards when litigating concurrently in district court and before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman brief contents and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Markman briefs are organized like typical briefs and usually contain: Introduction; Background (address technology of the patented invention); argument elements (discuss relevant claim construction law, describe a POSA, set out proposed constructions and supporting arguments); and Conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include proposed constructions for each disputed term and arguments based on intrinsic and any extrinsic evidence; consider attaching expert declaration or prerecorded tutorial and conform to local/judge-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and limit claim terms for construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigants should identify claim terms necessary for construction based on infringement and validity positions and the intrinsic/extrinsic evidence that supports their positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local patent rules or judges' rules may limit the number of terms (e.g., N.D. Cal. Local Pat. R. 4-3(c) attempts to limit to the most significant terms, up to ten); minimize terms to avoid diluting key disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer on disputed claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often require parties to meet and confer regarding disputed claim terms before submitting claim construction briefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the meet-and-confer to narrow disputes and agree where possible on terms with no real impact on case outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of Markman hearings is flexible and strategic
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that a court conduct a Markman hearing at a particular point; hearings can occur before, during or after fact or expert discovery and even during trial before jury instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early hearings can reduce litigation costs and narrow discovery but may lead to broader constructions and increased discovery; later hearings allow fuller development of arguments but may require experts to opine under competing constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct of Markman hearings: tutorials and oral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Markman hearings comprise a tutorial for the court on scientific background and oral argument for claim construction, which may include live witness testimony (inventor or experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some judges prefer live tutorials; others prefer tutorials in briefing. Be prepared to provide expert testimony if tutorials are not allowed live.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use demonstrative evidence effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Use demonstrative evidence because claim construction often involves complex scientific issues that the court must understand to reach a proper construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstratives include projector presentations to distill issues and physical boards that remain in the courtroom and visible to the judge; choose formats that best assist the judge's comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe local patent rules and judges' preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may have local patent rules governing timing, briefing, tutorials and other aspects of claim construction; judges may have individual preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check and tailor Markman briefs and hearing conduct to local rules and the judge's standing orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic goals and appealability of Markman rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful claim construction ruling can support summary judgment motions and often determines outcomes (jury instructions, infringement/validity). A district court's Markman ruling is not final and therefore is not immediately appealable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may stipulate to resolve remaining issues to obtain a final decision more quickly and enable appeal to the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent district court litigation and USPTO proceedings; stays
rubrics_metrics.description: When concurrent district court litigation and USPTO proceedings (e.g., inter partes review or post-grant review) exist, a party can move to stay district court proceedings pending USPTO resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court may grant a stay because a USPTO decision may affect district court outcomes; consider timing advantages from AIA-imposed USPTO deadlines that make stays more attractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for stay in covered business method (CBM) transitional program
rubrics_metrics.description: On a request for a stay when there are concurrent district court and USPTO proceedings involving business method patents, the district court can consider whether: a stay may simplify issues for trial; discovery is complete and a trial date is set; a stay presents a clear tactical advantage for the moving party and prejudices the nonmoving party; and a stay/denial may reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these four-part stay factors in the context of the specific case when deciding whether to seek or oppose a stay.
